paragraphs.text: I have read these verses, dear brethren, because they speak of a brother as a “fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience, in Jesus”. If there was one feature that was outstanding in our brother whom we have gathered here to bury, it was that of a brother; not only a brother in the way of sympathy among his brethren, but a brother who was prepared to take upon himself, feelingly, his full share of the burdens of the testimony. That, I believe, is in mind in this scripture, a brother who was a “fellow-partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and patience, in Jesus”.

Our brother was prepared to take his full share in this city in which we are—his full share of the burdens and the sorrows of the testimony in a day when many have turned aside, and when Pauline light, and the great result of Pauline ministry, have been given up. But there are those who are prepared to go on and, as fellow workers, to continue in the truth, in the testimony, at the high level upon which the Spirit of God would have it maintained in this closing day. I am sure we would all bear witness, dear brethren, that our brother has been one such.

The Spirit of God would use this occasion, as we are here at this burial, that we all may be stimulated, as persons who take our full share, as the word says, “Take thy share in suffering as a good soldier of Jesus Christ”, 2 Timothy 2: 3.

The days in which we are have seen so many turning away from the truth, and the particular character of the testimony in such days calls for suffering and for the feature of a soldier. The days call for the feature of patience, of being a fellow-partaker in the tribulation and in the kingdom. The opportunity is open (may the Spirit of God use this opportunity, dear brethren) for persons in this place to come forward to take their share in the burdens of the testimony for the Lord’s sake, at the close of the day.

John hears a voice behind him and he turns to see. It is a sorrowful thing to lose a brother at any time, but think of what it is in this place to lose one who took his full share in the burdens of the locality, and in the burdens of the testimony. Such a loss might well be overwhelming.

John says here, “I fell at his feet as dead; and he laid his right hand upon me”. I believe that the meaning of laying His right hand upon John was that there should be power in John to continue, despite all the history, and the way the Lord was moving. We are to see what He has in mind, that there may be power for continuance.

Therefore, dear brethren, this is not the end. It is the end in one sense—we are about to bury our brother—but it is not the end. It is intended to create a beginning in every one of us freshly to commit ourselves, with fresh resolve, to the testimony right on to the close of the day, no matter what sacrifice may be called for.

May we therefore be stimulated, dear brethren, in this service which is ours, to go on, no matter what the day may hold for us, and whatever the suffering may be. Let us remember the short period of the testimony of our brother—how much he has been marked by continuance and faithfulness, and by committal to carrying his full share in the testimony. May that be the portion of each one of us, until the end, for the Lord’s glory.

paragraphs.speaker: CR
text: The Spirit of God would give us a fresh and living impression, beloved brethren, at this time of sorrow, that Jesus does all things well. He always does all things well. As we say that, we say it with confidence. The persons who said it in the scripture we have read said it from observation— we say it thankfully from experience, that Jesus does all things well.

Our beloved brother has continued in the truth. He stood the test of 1970, and stood in the truth. He stood the test of 1972, and again stood in the truth. He faced the test of these recent days and weeks and months with all their weakness and sufferings. In all these tests he has witnessed by his spirit of thankfulness throughout that he knew that Jesus “does all things well”.

The Lord, with His own gracious touch, would give our beloved sister a fresh sense this very day that Jesus does all things well. Let us all have full confidence in Christ—“He does all things well”. There may be tests ahead for our beloved sister and her two daughters, but let them be strengthened in faith for each day and, whatever the tests, see that Jesus is still doing all things well.

Then, as the Lord thinks of the service of God and of the testimony, He is not unmindful as to how matters may proceed in this place. Let us be sure that, in the ways of God, the morning always follows the evening. If there be an evening of sorrow, of testing and of exercise, the Lord will enlarge on the joy and peace that always follow as far as the people of God are concerned. Undoubtedly we will all have been pleading with God as to how matters are going to proceed in this place. I think the answer is that, “He makes both the deaf to hear, and the speechless to speak”.

O, beloved, may the reality of this night of sorrow, of bereavement and pressure, make way for every one of us to receive some fresh touch of the Lord Jesus Himself; that we may hear some fresh word from Christ that will liberate us from everything that is holding us in our hearts, and cause us to speak in the service of God, and to speak in the testimony, until the Lord comes.

Out of this very evening may we be in full confidence that the morning is about to come, yea, maybe from this very day the morning is dawning when God will move in His mighty power and bring others into the service of God and into the testimony of God, and, through it all, bring the comfort of the Spirit to all the brethren, with the sense that God is having His own way.
Let us be steadied in the assurance and full unshakable confidence that, whatever outward circumstances may come, Jesus does all things well, for His name’s sake.
(Words given on the occasion of the burial of our beloved brother Mr. Ernest Jenner, Bromley. Notes of the first word are not available).

articles.title: “FILL THE WATER VESSELS WITH WATER”
articles.author: A. B. Parker
articles.place: Word on the occasion of a marriage, Brooklyn, N.Y

paragraphs.text: This scripture in John 2 has yielded much in its use at occasions like this. It has often been noted that the mother of Jesus was present and that “Jesus also, and his disciples, were invited”. Evidently it was a time when natural relationships tended to dominate. That tendency may readily obtain at a marriage, for there is the side of natural relationship which is ordained of God and has its place, but if happiness is to be a lasting matter, the natural must be controlled by the spiritual. We have been through much sorrow because this has not been so. Indeed, we are greatly tested at the present time because of the scattering that has taken place over assembly issues, and it is an exercise at this time whether the mixed conditions here will prevent the Lord from giving us a word.

I have in mind to call to our attention what the Lord said at that occasion in Cana of Galilee, trusting that He will have a word for us in it. He did not say much on that occasion. His mother had spoken, telling the servants to do whatever Jesus said to them. When told that wine was deficient, He said to the servants, “Fill the water-vessels with water”, and they filled them to the brim. It is the responsibility of servants to do what the Lord tells them to do. I desire to do just that. The word is, “Fill the water-vessels with water”. I would like to fill you to the brim!

The tremendous scattering which has taken place has been largely due to a lack of appreciation and use of the water. John’s gospel, which has a peculiar bearing on the last days, tells us much about the water, beginning with the baptism of John who said, “I baptise with water”, John 1: 26. Let us consider, briefly, what is said about water. We are told that John was baptising in AEnon near Salim, because there was a great deal of water there, John 3: 23. Have we applied the water in abundance in the practical working out of our baptism, or do we need to go back to our beginnings and see if there has been a lack of water? The abundance of water in the Red Sea was provided to wash away every vestige of what was Egyptian. The people were all baptised to Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Has the water been applied abundantly by us, practically, to wash the world, and our desires for it, out of our hearts? Then the Lord Jesus spoke to Nicodemus about being born anew and being born of water and of Spirit, John 3: 3–5. The very beginning of God’s work in us for the formation of the “inward man”, which is subject to the law of God, is related to being born of water and of Spirit. Has this been a real experience with us? The intent is that what is born anew in us may be preserved from defilement by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Then, in John 4, we are introduced to a Samaritan woman who, obviously, was a subject of new birth. The Lord speaks to her about His giving the living water—“The water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into eternal life”. Do you know what it is to have this wonderful spring in you, lifting you up into the enjoyment of eternal life

and participation in the service of God? The teaching clearly shows the direct relation of the water to the Holy Spirit, but we have our responsibility in all these relations, whether to maintain the separation which baptism indicates or to drink of the living water which the Lord gives. It is not just teaching, it involves experience.

Then the Lord Jesus introduces the water in chapter 13, to bring in the spiritual refreshment needed if we are to have part with Christ. The teaching is progressive. This reference is related to the Supper. “Jesus ... rises—from supper”, it says. He poured water into a wash-hand basin and began to wash the feet of His disciples. Have you known the Lord’s service to refresh you so as to have part with Him after the Supper on Lord’s day, so that you can worship the Father in spirit and in truth? I am going over these items quickly, not assuming to cover every reference to water in the gospel, but seeking to do as the Lord commanded—“Fill the water vessels with water”.

Finally, we come to the Lord’s sufferings an the cross. Can we consider this scene without depth of feeling? His agonies affect us. He suffered for us. He died, and a soldier pierced His side, and forthwith there came out blood and water, John 19: 34. What meaning that gives to the subject of the water! O, dear brethren, have we neglected the water? Our approach to God is based upon the blood and the water. Both came from His riven side. We draw near to God, “sprinkled as to our hearts from a wicked conscience”—that relates to the blood of Christ—“and washed as to our body with pure water” (Hebrews 10: 22)—that relates to the water which came from the side of Christ. How necessary is the water!

In the types in the Old Testament the ashes of the red heifer, which was burned in the presence of the priest (Numbers 19: 5), were used to give efficacy to the water of purification, which was required to remove uncleanness. It is also called the water of separation, Numbers 19: 13. If we are prepared to receive help from the Lord, we will acknowledge that diversions and differences which have come in are substantially due to lack of understanding, it may be, but surely due to lack of application, of the water spiritually. In Numbers 19, where the water of purification is made available for cleansing, the point is made that if the person who becomes defiled fails to use the water of purification, he defiles the tabernacle of Jehovah and must be separated from Israel. We should be affected by the serious way in which God looks at despising, or failure to use, the water of purification which has been made available at such a cost. The intensity of the burning of the red heifer is equal to the burning of the beasts whose blood is taken into the sanctuary on the day of atonement and sprinkled on the mercy-seat and before the mercy-seat to provide a place and standing for us in the presence of God.

This should help us to see the importance of cleansing our way. We are called upon to walk in separation from the world and to purify ourselves from every pollution of flesh and spirit, 2 Corinthians 7: 1. To disregard this is a slight, indeed a sin, against the sufferings of Christ. May we have the sense that the Lord is saying something to us and take heed to His word.

Well, dear brethren, I trust that the water-vessels have been filled with water. If so, that is not the end. The Lord Jesus spoke again—when the vessels were filled to the brim. He said, “Draw out now, and carry it to the feast-master”. Did they draw out water? No, they drew out wine—wine that surpassed anything they had known before. There had been a change. Where did the change occur? In the water-vessels. And if we accept the word the Lord has given, and act on it, there will be change in us. May we have the sense that the Lord has spoken, for God is not the Author of confusion, but of oneness. God is one—three Persons, but God is one. The oneness set out in divine Persons should be taken account of, for it is not God’s mind that we should be divided. After the change had taken place in the water-vessels all at the feast would drink of the new wine—all would be in the new-found joy which the change had brought about. May we all be concerned that we may not resist change, where needed, that we may be able to share the joy that the Lord would bring in.

But there may be some specific blessing that the Lord would bring in. While there is the general matter of the marriage celebration, there were six water-vessels. Who do the six vessels represent? They would be the principals at the marriage, possibly. There would be the bridegroom and the bride, certainly, but can we also say that the parents of the bridegroom and the bride may be represented? The Lord’s feelings toward the young couple would be compassionate and in the attitude of blessing. They have had soul history; they have been tested, and I believe that the Lord has helped them through the tests. I believe we can say that without hesitation. What about the father and mother of the bride?—and what about the father and the mother of the bridegroom? Does the Lord have a special word for them? Is there some change He would bring about in them? The change took place in the six water-vessels. How we would like to see whatever change is necessary to bring about the oneness of which we have been speaking.

I have been simple and plain in what I have said, but I have felt that the Lord laid something upon me. I trust that it is indeed so, and that we will hear what He has said. Are we prepared to embrace the precious meaning of the water that came from the side of Jesus? Are we prepared to cleanse our way, that we may walk in the path of God’s will? If so, we will surely drink of the water made wine, and I feel sure we will come into the experience of unity and oneness in the faith and in the fellowship practically. May the Lord grant that it may be so!

What I wish to draw attention to in these two passages is a scene of plenty, in contrast to dearth. The place where Mephibosheth was, Lodebar, means a place of no pasture. That may be the case in the state of persons’ souls. They may be surrounded by plenty in a material way and yet as to the state of their soul it may be for them a place of no pasture. David is enthroned in this passage. He is in the place of power. He is exercising his administration in favour of some who might be deemed unlikely persons, the last to be thought of by David. “Is there yet any left”, he says, “of the house of Saul?”. It was Saul who pursued David “as when they hunt a partridge on the mountains”, 1 Samuel 26: 20.

How the world has treated Christ we know very well. Men, especially religious persons, pursued Him relentlessly. Finally they cast Him out and crucified Him. When God in the Person of Christ came into this world, man, so far as he could and as soon as he could, turned Him out. What an issue that is! The statesmen of this world are engaged with what they consider to be the greatest issues, but this is greater. The issue is how the world has treated the Son of God and continues to treat Him. It says of some persons that they have trodden under foot the Son of God and crucify Him for themselves, and that they have insulted the Spirit of grace, Hebrews 6: 6 and 10: 29. These scriptures refer to apostates from christianity, persons who have been, or may be as yet, in the sphere of divine light where God’s name is known and revealed, and yet turn away from the light.

Well, it makes it all the more wonderful that David, typical of Christ, should be thinking of “any left of the house of Saul”, as much as to say, There may have been many who have come into the blessing, but there may be some who have not. “Is there yet any left?” I wonder if there is in this company anyone belonging, so to speak, to the house of Saul. There was one, this man Mephibosheth, a lame man; he had suffered an accident. Sometimes we say that his nurse dropped him, but Scripture does not say that. It says that he fell (2 Samuel 4: 4), and the fact is, dear friends, that every one of us comes from fallen stock. Not only are we sinners, but we are lost as to our estate as men and women according to the flesh, fallen. How wonderful it is that God tonight, from His throne an high, should have to say not only to guilty sinners but to fallen man.

We rather underestimate the significance of what we speak of as ‘the fall’. God made man and He put him in an environment bespeaking all the goodness of a Creator God, and man would rather believe the devil than God. He disobeyed God. The government of God followed. He drove man out of paradise, and he cannot get back again. Neither does God intend that he shall, not into that earthly paradise. Men may strive for it with all the inventiveness, all the capacity and all the resources that they have. They may try to produce an earthly paradise, but God has no intention that man should be reinstated in an earthly paradise, in innocence. God’s thought is not man in innocence but man in righteousness. Hymn 212 says, ‘Man in righteousness is there’. Christ is in heaven, and others are going to be there, because He is there.

Now into this scene of plenty a man was brought from a distance, and not only brought, but it says he came. He came to David. He was not an unwilling person. It is a great thing to be willing when God appeals, when He touches your conscience and reaches your heart. “Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power”, Psalm 110: 3. Here is one of those who are willing. What kind of a man is he? A king’s son, of royal lineage. You could speak of ‘the glories of his blood and state’, but they are shadows, not substantial. Here is a lame prince, coming to David. Will you come to Jesus? He came, a king’s son. He says, “Such a dead dog as I am”. That was his own estimate of himself. As another said once, ‘All the bark and the bite had gone out of him’; not only a dog, but a dead one. It was the Syrophoenician woman who spoke of the dogs. “Even the dogs”, she said, “eat of the crumbs which fall from the table of their masters”, Matthew 15: 27. Would grace meet such a condition? Surely it would. Is that condition here? “Such a dead dog as I am”. I might say, ‘I am sorry for the thing I did, I will not do it again’. It would be right to say that, to judge myself for what I have done. But to judge myself for what I am is a much deeper thing.

Such a man was Mephibosheth. He says, ‘I am of the worst kind’. David said, ‘Nothing but the best for you’. He is to be brought into a scene of plenty. He is to enjoy high society, not earthly, but heavenly, the king’s sans and the king’s table, and to eat bread continually there. Do you know anything that the world can offer to be compared with that—to eat bread continually in suited company in the presence of the King and at His table? This is the blessing in the heart of God for a repentant sinner. You say, It speaks of the greatest consideration for the sinner—and surely it does; but the point is, it is David’s delight to do it, as it was the father’s delight in Luke 15 to have the son clothed in the best robe. It was for the father’s pleasure. The son would have said, “Make me as one of thy hired servants”. He had no sense at that time of what was in the heart of his father, and it is a fact that many christians have not a full sense of what is in the Father’s heart in blessing.

Now the gospel comes to us that we might be enlightened as to these things and responsive to them. So Mephibosheth is brought into this wonderful setting as a king’s son and to sit at David’s table and, mark this, to eat bread continually. He would not willingly miss any meeting. He certainly would not miss lightly the breaking of bread, to eat bread in that sense.

What a privilege! Think of the claim the Lord Jesus has upon us, that we are His, fruit of redemption. His claim is paramount. He said before He died, “This do in remembrance of me”, 1 Corinthians 11: 24. One cannot understand how a true believer can fail to do it, how anyone could be indifferent to the appeal of the love of Christ to call Him to mind. It was said of the cup-bearer in Joseph’s day that he forgot Joseph. How could you forget? The Lord does not forget us. He has never forgotten us for a moment. His saints are always in His heart, every one of them. God says through His prophet, “Can a woman forget her sucking child ... Even these forget, but I will not forget thee”, Isaiah 49: 15. And it is so. There is no mother, however much she loves her child, but at some moment or another the child is out of her mind; it cannot be otherwise. But God says of His people, “I will not forget thee”. O, what a thing it is to know God, revealed in Jesus!

Now in Joseph’s case we have a state of things which is described as “exceeding much”. In the seven years of plenty “the land brought forth by handfuls”. It was so much that they left off numbering. It says “it was without number”. And yet it brought forth “by handfuls”.

There was that which could be appropriated by any person who had a hand, even if their hand was quite a small one, a boy’s hand or a girl’s hand. You know these things are for boys and girls. You say, ‘My hand is very small, and my heart is small’. Would you like Jesus to fill them, to fill your hand with Himself, and your heart? He has great regard for young people of all ages, even quite small people, small enough to take up in His arms. It says at one point, “Having taken them in his arms … he blessed them”, Mark 10: 15.

Then there were older ones. One of them had died. His mother was a widow; he was the only son of his mother and they were carrying him out to bury him. The Lord spoke to him as they carried him out on the bier and said, “Youth, I say to thee, Wake up”, Luke 7: 14. O, we long that the youth of the present day may hear the voice of Christ! He is speaking to youth, not only to old people, or very young people, but to youth. “Youth, I say to thee, Wake up. And the dead sat up and began to speak”, and it says that Jesus “gave him to his mother”. That is, he was not left by the roadside, nor was he handed over to someone else, he was put where there was affection for him. Persons who are blessed in that sense are put in an environment where there is affection. The mother is there. “Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother”, Galatians 4: 26

Well, I am speaking of Joseph. It says that “he gathered up all the food of the seven years”. What years they must have been!—like the days of Jesus. You read the gospels and you get some sense of the food of the seven years, the handfuls of it, and how much was there—more than is recorded. John says, “And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which if they were written one by one, I suppose that not even the world itself would contain the books written”, John 21: 25. It is like what they did here, “they left off numbering; for it was without number”. I should like our hearts to get a real sense tonight of this scene of plenty, this wonderful administration of wealth and of food. It is not always a question of food. The Lord has other things. He says to some, “I counsel thee to buy of me gold purified by fire … and white garments … and eye-salve”, Revelation 3: 18. These things the Lord has, and you can have them on the simple principle of coming to Him and having to do with Him. “Buy of me”; there are no agents in that sense, there is no representation. It is a question, dear friends, of a personal transaction with the Saviour.

It was so here with Joseph. It says, “The people cried to Pharaoh for bread; and Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, Go to Joseph “(Genesis 41: 55). That is where it is. How he managed to deal with all those thousands, maybe hundreds of thousands, of people we do not know, but they had to go to him. Notice that, Pharaoh says, “What he says to you, that do”. That is important. Many would like to have the blessing and then go off in the pursuit of what pleases them, but that is not God’s thought. Certainly He desires that you may have the blessing, but then that you may come under the direction and the control of our Lord Jesus Christ. “What he says to you, that do”. The Lord has great affairs, great operations, on hand, and He will have persons to engage with Him in what He is doing, as with David when some came and he said, “If ye come peaceably to me to help me, my heart shall be knit unto you; but if to betray me …”, then it would not be so (1 Chronicles 12: 17). But then one man answered, “Thine we are, David”. He said that in the power of the Spirit, and as soon as you come under the domination of Christ you find what a resource you have in the Holy Spirit.
Do not think that the Spirit is given to persons who are not prepared to accept the lordship of Christ. “What he says to you, that do”.

Well, dear friends, that is all I have to say. We have these two scenes of plenty, one involving a company of persons at the king’s table, eating bread continually; the other the opening of these storehouses, the only places where provision was. The death of Christ has laid bare the heart of God, and what a place of provision we find that to be! “They shall be abundantly satisfied with the fatness of thy house; and thou wilt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures”, Psalm 36: 8.

These passages refer to the gate of Bethlehem. It can be shown that in Scripture the gate refers, to the place of discrimination and judgment, where matters affecting city welfare are dealt with. Nowadays men have transferred this function to town halls and committee rooms, often meeting in secret session. But the city gate was evidently a public place and justice could be seen to be done; it could be looked at and inspected and would stand, as we say, the light of day. In a day to come the holy city will be seen, with its twelve gates and the administration of Christ, and its benign influence will spread universally. What an administration it will be! You, dear fellow believer, will have a part in that administration and your influence then will be co-relative to your influence now. Hence it is important that you and I should know something about the gate by experience now and that we should not evade our responsibility in that regard.

I fear that we may sometimes opt out of our responsibility. That is what Elimelech did; he opted for the relative ease of life in the country of Moab. There would be no assembly sorrows to carry there, but there would be no assembly joys either. I ask myself, do I carry my share of responsibility in my place? If I miss a meeting do I decline responsibility for what transpired in it? If I am unavoidably absent—I hope it is never the other way—do I enquire as to what went on? In the ordering of things, such as the arrangements of family life, some persons may often have to miss being present. Do you then, dear sister, enquire what the reading was like? And do you, dear brother, tell her, even if she forgets to enquire? One thing that becomes evident as this book proceeds is that Naomi always wanted to know, when Ruth returned home, how she had got on. On one occasion Ruth brought home six measures of barley (Ruth 3: 17). I wonder if I could do that—take home such a large impression of Christ. Boaz had measured that to her; it was what could be contained in her cloak. How she had grown since leaving Moab!

Bethlehem does not set out the public glory that will be seen in the holy city. It was small and apparently had only one gate, at least I think it is always spoken of in the singular. Many localities are like that; they are small, and it is not until you enter them that you realise what vital things are proceeding there. But though it was small it had a gate, and that gate was in function. That itself was a remarkable thing, considering the general current of the time, when every man did what was right in his own eyes. In those days an observant traveller passing through the land would have been able to sum up the general situation that obtained. It is not too difficult to observe the general situation in christendom today. But suppose that traveller had happened to come across Bethlehem; he would have found what was remarkably different, so different that he would have wondered. He would not have known what obtained there unless he saw for himself. He might, of course, hear by report, but reports can be untrue, as we very well know. He would need to go there himself to find out the truth; there were right relations obtaining there; there was barley, there was wheat, and there was the functioning of the gate.

Do you think such a place can be found today? God will have things millennially, of course; we would all subscribe to that. But do you not think he would give a testimony somewhere (and those who seek will find) to the same principles operating now that will obtain then?

Think of Solomon’s reign—it somewhat typifies the millennial reign of Christ. One outstanding feature was those two pillars which stood out in front of the house. One of them was called Boaz. Yes, you say, of course Christ will be outstanding then. But in Bethlehem Boaz is outstanding now! Is He not to be found, actively moving and completing His matters? Because Bethlehem is small, is He not to be found there? Does He not go forth from there, Micah 5: 2? Great things, beloved, can be found in smallness.

I suppose the commandments had been written on the gate of Bethlehem, as envisaged in Deuteronomy 6: 9. When Elimelech and Naomi had gone out to Moab they would have had their backs turned to those commandments. Alas, there have been many like that! Elimelech got into a false position; someone else was king to him in spite of his name (‘Whose God is king’). He represents mere profession. I may profess to be governed by God, yet my movements show otherwise. That element is in all of us; may we face it and learn to judge it.

Naomi represents another element, one which accepts and feels deeply the consequences of departure from God; may that remain with us! Ruth signifies yet another element, that of affections formed and developed by the Spirit; may these increase with us! If we are honest we will find, I think, all these elements within us. Which will become dominant? Eventually Elimelech dies; how sorrowful! He died out of fellowship. We have sorrowfully witnessed that this has happened in our own day and it is peculiarly poignant to think of a brother or a sister for whom you had great regard not being recovered to the testimony before death. But Naomi, now clear of the element which Elimelech represents, sets her face towards Bethlehem. In doing this she showed clearly that she sought her country (Hebrews 11: 14).

There is room, I believe, for this experience to be known again. When she got to Bethlehem the brethren remembered her, “all the city was moved” (Ruth 1: 19). Has this not been recently known, dear brethren? She would have found that the same good commandments still remained on the gate. Nothing would have been scratched out or painted over, nor any modifying comments added, such as ‘This one not now workable in a broken day’. No, she would find nothing of God given up, and the barley harvest in immediate prospect, with the wheat to follow.

But coming back involves responsibility, too. If Bethlehem conditions are to be preserved it will involve my developing a right power of discernment and judgment, in principle supporting the gate. Perhaps in this lies the secret of maintaining good conditions, that everyone carries local responsibility and is vitally in what proceeds. Boaz says, “all the gate of my people knows” (Ruth 3: 11). We may feel that we do not reach this yet in our localities, but let us set ourselves for it. At the end of the book such conditions eventuate in a worshipper. Your undivided affection and loyalty for Christ will sustain you, and your measure will grow.

In chapter 3 Ruth risked her reputation with others; the overriding consideration was that, typically, she must have to do with Christ for herself. Do not be put off, dear brother or sister, by what others may say; you move to Christ for yourself. If He says you are virtuous, that is everything, and it is a great thing to be delivered from the opinions of others. One is not saying that conditions in Bethlehem were perfect. In fact, Scripture rather suggests that one brother there was perhaps a little self-centred, a thing not unknown to most of us. Do you say, ‘I am looking for the perfect company’? Suppose you found it; do you think it would still remain perfect after you came? What is important is that, whilst things were not perfect in Bethlehem, divine principles were not only subscribed to but were also being applied, and the passage describing the enactment of the redemption of Ruth is one of the most beautiful in the whole of Scripture.

Now in 2 Samuel 23 we have another setting. Others have pointed out that in 1 Chronicles 11 the mighty men are listed at the beginning of David’s reign, but in Samuel they appear at the end. Will there be such at the end of our dispensation? The passage read speaks of a peculiar kind of mightiness. Sometimes we think that mightiness is seen in the power to sway persons, maybe even to slay them! But this section describes a different kind of mightiness, one which lies in satisfying the longings of Christ. Those longings stand related to what is in the gate, and if you want to satisfy them you must get there. Do you see what this means? You must break through. Maybe your lethargy holds you; maybe you are more tainted with Moab than you think. The Lord Jesus asked you to remember Him in the way that He ordered and His longings, I say again, are related to the gate, to a system of ordered administration and judgment, and one which makes wholesome demands upon you. You cannot properly take part in His service unless you support the principles of right judgment. There were possibly other wells in the vicinity, but you must get to the one that is in the gate. It is so specified twice over, it is that particular well. There were few here that did it; will you be among them? The Lord, typically, takes this water—it is the result of a spiritual exploit—and presents it to God. It is very beautiful, and it is thus that the service of God is properly carried on.

May these passages, dear brethren, become meaningful to us. They were written for us and I venture to suggest that they show that the carrying out of local responsibility provides a good groundwork for the service of God to develop in reality. May the Lord help us, for His name’s sake.

It becomes very solemn to consider that the commercial system heads up in the king of Tyre, who is a type of Satan himself. It is right that the people of God, having necessarily to do directly or indirectly with commerce, should be warned as to progressing in it beyond what is necessary. If we aim at anything beyond that, we place ourselves within the range of the god of this world. In handling the creatures of God commercially for a livelihood, you can give God thanks, but going beyond that into the spirit of Tyre in competition and ambition is dangerous; it means we are brought under the influence of the god of this world ...

If I can supply, through commerce, the means of helping the people of God, as Hiram did in David’s and Solomon’s day, that is a justifiable thing; but when I go beyond that, and amass the means of living in affluence and leave God out, I put myself within the range of the god of this world.
